discovery.title: What can cargo reveal when a 4,500-year-old ship has vanished?
discovery.summary: Archaeologists say pottery from a wreck near Kekova Island may date to roughly 4,500 years ago. The wooden vessel has not survived; its cargo offers clues to early Mediterranean trade.
discovery.why_it_matters: If the dating holds, the site could add evidence about seafaring and exchange during the Early Bronze Age. Researchers say more work is needed.

discovery.title: Can giant redwoods keep absorbing carbon as heat stresses their leaves?
discovery.summary: A study reported this week found that California coast redwood leaves slow photosynthesis during heat spikes, raising questions about how warming affects these forests’ carbon uptake.
discovery.why_it_matters: Redwoods store substantial carbon; heat stress could affect forest health and the role these forests play in climate systems.

discovery.title: Can cities save stormwater for the next drought?
discovery.summary: A new report describes an EU-backed Sponge Facility intended to help cities adopt green spaces, permeable surfaces and storage that capture and reuse rainwater.
discovery.why_it_matters: Urban water systems face both flooding and drought. Retaining rain locally could reduce runoff while improving water resilience, though outcomes depend on implementation.

discovery.title: Does the brain develop from one starting cell population—or two?
discovery.summary: A study highlighted this week challenges a traditional model of brain development, suggesting distinct cell populations contribute to different brain regions. The work may inform how researchers grow brain cells in the lab.
discovery.why_it_matters: A better map of brain development could shape basic research and lab models, but the finding does not yet establish a medical application.
